stories.summary: A wicked witch with great power decides to play with humankind. She makes every material good on Earth vanish, leaving 7.3 billion naked people on the planet. But she leaves all knowledge intact in their heads — and tells them they get everything back the moment they build her one working iPhone 6S. The question: how many years would it take? On the Lex Fridman podcast, Urban led into it via Leonard Read's 'I, Pencil' — that no single human knows how to make a pencil, let alone a smartphone.
stories.insight: The whole episode's frame: civilisation isn't a stockpile of objects, it's a fragile choreography of distributed and tacit knowledge. Strip away the institutions, supply chains and accumulated artefacts and the 'knowledge in our heads' is suddenly far smaller and more useless than we imagined.

stories.topic: What Would Actually Happen — A Crash To 10 Million Humans
stories.summary: Ajay's answer to Urban's experiment is unsentimental. Civilisation could not feed 7.5 billion people without markets, factories, food processing and institutions, so first humanity would descend into 'a post-apocalyptic novel' (he reaches for Cormac McCarthy's *The Road*). The witch would be long forgotten, the population would crash to ~10 million, and only out of that ruin would a brand-new scientific civilisation slowly grow. We'd eventually rebuild communications technology, but never the *exact* iPhone 6S — that precise journey to semiconductors and touch screens is gone.
stories.insight: The hidden infrastructure of modernity isn't recoverable from individual brains alone. Knowledge depends on the matching scaffolding of institutions, prices, laws and physical capital — and history's particular path is not deterministic; the same civilisation cannot be replayed.

stories.topic: The Solitary Confinement Project — Rebuilding Mathematics From Axioms
stories.summary: Ajay's recurring thought experiment: if you were thrown into solitary confinement with only paper and pen, no books, what would you do to stay sane and reach the flow state? His answer is a Whitehead-Russell-style project — start from axioms and try to recreate as much of mathematics as possible. He knows a lot of mathematics, but only as 'mere beliefs' propped up by reference books; without proofs, those beliefs are nothing. The discipline is to honour the shared inheritance of 500 years of mathematics by trying to rederive it from scratch.
stories.insight: A model of intellectual humility. Most of what we 'know' is actually trust in chains we've never personally walked. Stress-testing your knowledge by trying to rederive it reveals how thin the part you truly own actually is.

stories.topic: Silphium — The Roman Super-Spice Lost For Two Millennia
stories.summary: The Romans wrote everything down, and they waxed eloquent about silphium — a plant from what is now Libya, whose resinous gum was the food of the gods. They never managed to cultivate it; foragers gathered it from the wild, where it commanded the highest prices. Within a couple of hundred years it was gone — Pliny the Elder records that the last single stalk was given to Emperor Nero. For 20 years, Ajay says, he's felt the hurt of that loss. Then a Turkish scientist found a plant in remote Greece and Turkey that fits the descriptions; he is quietly cultivating it in greenhouses (lest a foraging stampede on eBay drive it extinct again) before scaling it up as an exotic herb. The Romans also wrote of a cheap substitute — asafoetida (hing), also a *Ferula* species — connecting the lost herb to a staple of Indian cooking.
stories.insight: Knowledge survives best when written, archived, and physically sampled. Even so, biological knowledge can vanish completely; what saves us is the combinatorial possibility of new tools (greenhouse cultivation, DNA, satellite imagery) plus the ancient written record. Recovery is rare, slow, and contingent.

stories.topic: Dhaka Muslin — The Disappeared Cloth The British Couldn't Reverse-Engineer
stories.summary: Dhaka muslin, woven from a cotton variety found on the banks of the Megna in Bengal, had ~1200 interlocking threads per square inch (modern muslin has 20-40). It was so diaphanous that a 19th-century European satire had a milliner tell a lady that to be well-dressed she had to be well-undressed. Production required deep specialisation across sixteen villages, each handling one part. When the trade collapsed, that knowledge vanished within a generation. A modern revival project found a 19th-century leaf in a London herbarium, did DNA analysis, used satellite imagery on the Megna's banks to find candidate plants (one shared 70% of the original DNA), and then went weaver-to-weaver across Bangladesh begging someone to attempt 1200-thread weaving. One agreed; they put him in a temperature-controlled hut (modern jugaad replacing the natural climate of the 16 villages); he made a 300-thread cloth. Dresses now sell for thousands of dollars — but 300 to 1200 is still a long way.
stories.insight: Tradition that lives in distributed hands and bodies, with no central scribe, can be irretrievably lost in a single generation. What rescues it is the British habit of obsessive sampling and record-keeping (the herbarium, the V&A) plus modern technologies (DNA, satellite imagery, climate control) — recovery is partial and expensive even so.

stories.topic: Fogbank — When The US Lost The Recipe For Its Own Nuclear Aerogel
stories.summary: Aerogels are the lightest known materials — a litre might weigh two or three grams. For a particular American atomic bomb, an aerogel codenamed 'Fogbank' was developed 40-50 years ago. During a major nuclear-weapons overhaul a decade or so back, the US discovered it had run out of fogbank inventory. The scientists of today went to the archives — project reports, scientific papers, experimental logs — and could not reproduce it. They then dragged in retired scientists, gave them their own old documents, and said 'you bloody now deliver.' Even those 'old hippies' couldn't pull it off. With auditors furious, the US spent ~$70 million on a brand-new research project to derive an equivalent aerogel from scratch. (Ajay also notes the speculation that Russia may not have a single working nuclear weapon today — because Soviet collapse-era loss of maintenance know-how would have compounded over twenty years.)
stories.insight: Even with the most disciplined documentation regime in human history (US Department of Energy nuclear-weapons production), tacit knowledge that isn't actively practised vanishes within a generation. If you stop *doing* something, you stop knowing it — paper alone will not save you.

stories.topic: The Painted Bench — A Parable About Tacit Knowledge In Institutions
stories.summary: An army camp has a 24/7 guard rota for a random bench in the middle of a field. A new commandant asks why. The guard doesn't know — he was just told to stand there. The deputy doesn't know. The previous commandant doesn't know. The commandant before him doesn't know. Obsessed, the new man flies economy across the country to a tiny farm where the now-93-year-old founder of the camp lies bedridden. He asks his one question. The wizened founder looks up: 'What are you saying? The paint hasn't dried yet.'
stories.insight: Institutions accumulate practices whose original purpose has been lost — the rationale evaporates while the ritual persists. Documentation isn't enough; without active interrogation, organisations carry forward zombie procedures decoupled from any real reason.

stories.topic: Tu Youyou And The Cold Extraction Of Wormwood
stories.summary: In 1974, in the middle of the Vietnam War, a non-PhD Chinese researcher named Tu Youyou was sent to Vietnam to help with malaria. Plasmodium had begun to resist quinine; she was physically moved by the suffering she saw. She remembered claims in ancient Chinese texts about cures for malaria. ~2000 plants from those texts had already been tested and dismissed as useless — including wormwood. But Tu was a master of classical Chinese, and she read a key sentence more carefully than others: it suggested *cold* extraction (a handful of plant in about a litre of water, no heat), not the boiling-water extraction scientists had defaulted to. She tried it. All twenty patients in her trial recovered. That breakthrough became artemisinin — today the front-line treatment for malaria worldwide.
stories.insight: Three lessons fused: (a) the credentialism filter would have excluded Tu; pure curiosity moved by empathy is the most powerful research package in the world; (b) language and close reading can recover knowledge a thousand other readers missed; (c) ancient texts have a low hit rate but their hits can be civilisation-altering.

stories.topic: Half The Top-20 Drugs Came From The Aborigines
stories.summary: Citing James C. Scott's *Seeing Like a State*, Ajay notes that out of the world's top 20 most important drugs, half have plant origins from traditional knowledge — quinine from South American aborigines, artemisinin from China, metformin from a European flower, and so on. Coffee was discovered because an Ethiopian shepherd noticed his goats getting unusually frisky after eating the berries; gorillas with stomach upsets walk 15 km to find a particular plant, and aborigines learned by watching them. Modern science has refined, dosed and industrialised these inputs, but the seed knowledge came from people we are condescending about.
stories.insight: Modernity overcredits its own fabrication. A huge fraction of what saves our lives today came from forest knowledge accumulated over millennia — knowledge that is now disappearing in a generation as forest peoples vanish. Preserving it is not nostalgia; it is preserving a working laboratory.

stories.topic: Germany And Japan Rose Like A Phoenix
stories.summary: By 1945, Germany and Japan were physically annihilated — every factory gone, cities firebombed, institutions taken over by the Nazis and then destroyed in war. And yet, in West Germany the brain power of one of the great technological civilisations of the 20th century survived (in 1933 Germany had more Nobel laureates than the United States). The Marshall Plan provided capital and books; West Germany's old shareholders had their pre-war Volkswagen shares honoured; an old Weimar-era constitutional draft was dusted off, infused with pacifism, and became the new constitution. Both countries went through truth-and-reconciliation phases, decisively turning their backs on nationalism and militarism. Standing in 1945, Ajay says, no one would have predicted how completely they would take off.
stories.insight: When the underlying human capital, books and norms are intact, physical destruction can be reversed within a generation. East Germany — same starting people, communist institutions — proves the mirror image: institutions, not stones, are the binding constraint.

stories.topic: Ludwig Erhard — The Right Man In The Right Place
stories.summary: Amit credits Ludwig Erhard, West Germany's finance minister 1949-1962 under Adenauer, as one of the great men of the 20th century. Erhard had lived through the Weimar Republic and understood the value of freedom — strong rule of law combined with property rights and space for individuals and firms to flourish. From a low base of total destruction, his free-market policies enabled the Wirtschaftswunder. 'All the things we would dream of for India,' Amit says, 'actually happened.'
stories.insight: Recovery from ruin still depends on getting the policy framework right at the critical moment. Knowledge of how prosperity actually works — diffuse markets, rule of law, property rights — is itself the most fragile and consequential body of knowledge a society can hold onto.

recommendations.creator: Tim Urban
recommendations.context: Urban's Wait But Why piece posing the wicked-witch experiment that frames the entire episode.
recommendations.reason: The cleanest way to feel in your gut how thin our personal knowledge actually is — and how much of 'what we know' is really 'what civilisation knows for us.'

recommendations.item: Tim Urban on The Lex Fridman Podcast
recommendations.creator: Tim Urban with Lex Fridman
recommendations.context: Urban explores the same iPhone thought experiment on Fridman's show.
recommendations.reason: Fridman's instinctive answer (a thousand engineers could build one) gets dismantled live as Urban pulls in metals, mining, cranes — a useful watch-along to the written piece.

recommendations.creator: Leonard Read
recommendations.context: First-person account of how a humble pencil is made, written from the pencil's point of view.
recommendations.reason: The original parable for the miracle of dispersed knowledge: no one person on Earth knows how to make a pencil, yet billions exist. The deepest cure for hubris about what 'we' know.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's 1945 essay arguing that prices are how dispersed knowledge gets aggregated.
recommendations.reason: The theoretical scaffolding under 'I, Pencil' — once you read it, you cannot stop seeing prices as a miraculous communication system. Featured in EIE's earlier 'Four Papers That Changed The World' episode.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed The World (Episode 41, Everything Is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Earlier EIE episode covering Hayek's paper among others.
recommendations.reason: The companion deep-dive into Hayek's 'Use of Knowledge in Society' for anyone who wants to follow the thread.

recommendations.creator: Cormac McCarthy
recommendations.context: Post-apocalyptic novel, a father and son crossing a ruined world.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's mental image of what Tim Urban's witch experiment would actually look like in practice — a vivid stand-in for civilisational collapse.

recommendations.creator: Stefan Zweig
recommendations.context: Zweig's novella of a man imprisoned in solitary confinement who plays chess against himself until he beats the world champion.
recommendations.reason: A literary companion to Ajay's solitary-confinement thought experiment — and a quiet warning that even genius isolation hits a ceiling without conversation and osmosis.

recommendations.creator: Philip Larkin
recommendations.context: Larkin's poem famously beginning 'They fuck you up, your mum and dad.'
recommendations.reason: Source of the line 'man hands on misery to man, it deepens like a coastal shelf' — Amit borrows it as the metaphor for knowledge accumulation, with the twist that 'sedimentary layers' can also be washed away.

recommendations.item: This miracle plant was eaten into extinction 2000 years ago — or was it?
recommendations.creator: Taras Grescoe
recommendations.context: National Geographic piece on the silphium rediscovery story.
recommendations.reason: The full account of the Turkish researcher's quiet rediscovery of a Ferula species in remote Greece and Turkey, and the careful greenhouse cultivation under way.

recommendations.item: The ancient fabric that no one knows how to make
recommendations.creator: Zaria Gorvett
recommendations.context: BBC piece on the lost art and partial revival of Dhaka muslin.
recommendations.reason: The story Amit followed down the rabbit hole — covers the 18th-century scandal, the 1200-thread thread-counts, and the modern reverse-engineering project.

recommendations.creator: Wikipedia contributors
recommendations.context: Encyclopaedia entry on the classified aerogel material used in US nuclear weapons.
recommendations.reason: The publicly available account of how a top-secret know-how vanished even from a defence-grade record-keeping system, costing tens of millions to recover.

recommendations.item: From bark to weed: The history of artemisinin
recommendations.creator: Claude Faurant
recommendations.context: Peer-reviewed historical paper on artemisinin's discovery and development.
recommendations.reason: The technical backstory to Tu Youyou's cold-extraction breakthrough and how the active sequence inside the molecule was later refined into modern derivatives.

recommendations.item: Tu Youyou on the Nobel Prize website
recommendations.creator: Nobel Prize Outreach
recommendations.context: Profile of Tu Youyou's life and Nobel-winning work.
recommendations.reason: A short, official source for the woman behind artemisinin — useful corrective to the 'no PhD, no credentials' bias and a reminder that empathy plus close reading can rewrite global health.

recommendations.creator: James C. Scott
recommendations.context: Scott's classic on how state legibility projects often destroy local knowledge.
recommendations.reason: Source of the claim that ~half of the top-20 most important modern drugs trace back to traditional plant knowledge — and a deeper argument for why aboriginal forest knowledge deserves protection.

recommendations.item: Beware of Quacks. Alternative Medicine Is Injurious to Health
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on the dangers of unscientific medicine.
recommendations.reason: His own argument for being deeply sceptical (but never dismissive) of tradition — including the mechanisms of reversion to the mean, confirmation bias and placebo that keep quackery alive.

recommendations.creator: Ben Goldacre
recommendations.context: Goldacre's takedown of bad medical reasoning and pseudoscience.
recommendations.reason: The book Amit reaches for to teach the discipline of double-blind randomised controlled trials — why a medicine must beat placebo, not just nothing.

recommendations.creator: Simon Singh and Edzard Ernst
recommendations.context: Empirical assessment of alternative medicine claims.
recommendations.reason: Companion to Goldacre — a careful, evidence-by-evidence walk through which 'traditional' remedies actually work and which don't.

recommendations.item: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Abby Philips
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive with the doctor known as the 'Liver Doc.'
recommendations.reason: A long-form Indian conversation about quackery, regulatory failures and the placebo trap — perfect listening alongside Goldacre and Singh-Ernst.

recommendations.creator: Tony Judt
recommendations.context: Judt's monumental history of Europe after 1945.
recommendations.reason: The masterwork on what reconstruction of Europe actually looked like — the human and institutional capital that came back, and the ethnic cleansing 'horrible nightmare' that ran from 1945 to 1948.

recommendations.item: On the Natural History of Destruction
recommendations.creator: W.G. Sebald
recommendations.context: Sebald's essays on the Allied bombing of German cities and Germany's silence about it.
recommendations.reason: A 'masterpiece' that fuses photographs and prose. Amit also takes it as an inspiration for what a modern multimedia solo essay-vlog could look like.

recommendations.creator: Pallavi Aiyar
recommendations.context: Aiyar's travelogue and essays on Japan.
recommendations.reason: A 'spectacularly good writer' on Japanese culture — a fine companion volume to the post-war Japan story for readers who want texture beyond economics.

recommendations.item: Pallavi Aiyar Has Seen the World (Episode 351, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pallavi Aiyar
recommendations.context: Amit's long-form conversation with the writer.
recommendations.reason: The audio companion to Orienting — Aiyar on her years in China, Indonesia, Japan and what it does to a mind to keep moving.

recommendations.creator: Isaac Asimov
recommendations.context: Asimov's classic short story.
recommendations.reason: Amit refuses to say more — saying any more would be a spoiler. A fitting close to an episode about civilisations that lose what they once knew.

core_ideas.concept: Knowledge As Coastal Shelf — But With Erosion
core_ideas.explanation: Borrowing Larkin's image, Amit reframes knowledge accumulation as sedimentary layering — but unlike the standard 'standing on the shoulders of giants' picture, the ocean of time washes layers away. Some knowledge survives, much is lost, some is regained. The episode is a tour through that erosion. The naive view that knowledge only grows is the very illusion the episode is built to break.
core_ideas.quote: Man hands on misery to man, it deepens like a coastal shelf. — Philip Larkin

core_ideas.concept: Tacit Knowledge And The Practice Constraint
core_ideas.explanation: A surprisingly large amount of working know-how can never be fully written down. The Fogbank story shows that even US Department of Energy nuclear-weapons records — among the most fastidiously documented in the world — could not reproduce a 40-year-old aerogel; even retired scientists handed their own original notes back couldn't make it work. The Dhaka muslin story makes the same point on the artisan side. The knowledge lives in continuous practice — the moment a generation stops *doing* it, the recovery cost balloons or becomes impossible.
core_ideas.quote: If you don't do something for 30-40 years, then there is a whole range of tacit knowledge that gets lost.

core_ideas.concept: Social Technology Is As Important As Hardware Technology
core_ideas.explanation: When Lex Fridman casually said a thousand engineers could rebuild an iPhone, Tim Urban pushed him on metals, mining, cranes. Ajay extends the point: progress isn't only technology, it's *social* technology — prices being a miraculous communication device that shares information and incentives across millions of strangers. Hayek's 'Use of Knowledge in Society' is the foundational text. Without prices, markets, property rights, rule of law, the underlying engineering knowledge has nothing to plug into.
core_ideas.quote: A stepping block of progress is not just technology, but also what I would call social technology.

core_ideas.concept: Recovery Requires The Right Records — And The Right Modern Tools
core_ideas.explanation: Across the lost-knowledge stories, the pattern of partial recovery is consistent: it took written archives (Pliny on silphium, V&A samples of Dhaka muslin), physical samples (a 19th-century leaf in a London herbarium), *and* modern tools that didn't exist before (DNA sequencing, satellite imagery, greenhouse cultivation, climate-controlled huts) to even begin to recreate the lost knowledge. Recovery is combinatorial — you need the relics *and* the new instruments. Without one of them, the knowledge stays gone.
core_ideas.quote: We have those cloth samples in the Victoria and Albert Museum. It's just that we don't know how to make them.

core_ideas.concept: Skeptical But Never Dismissive Of Tradition
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's stance: roughly half the top-20 modern drugs come from traditional plant knowledge, but ~2000 plants in classical Chinese texts were tested and dismissed before artemisinin landed. Tradition is mostly noise plus a few civilisation-changing signals. The mechanisms keeping quackery alive are reversion to the mean (a cold gets better either way), confirmation bias (you only count the times it 'worked'), and the powerful placebo effect. The right discipline is the double-blind RCT — a medicine must beat placebo, not just nothing.
core_ideas.quote: Respect tradition, but always be skeptical.

core_ideas.concept: The Hit-Rate Asymmetry Of Ancient Texts
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing: ancient texts are 'cool and funny... intended as humor' with the occasional nugget of mind-blowing truth. The hit rate is low. But the few hits — quinine, artemisinin, metformin, coffee — are world-altering, which justifies enormous investment in close reading and rigorous testing. The asymmetry is what made Tu Youyou's career: classical Chinese fluency to read more carefully than other researchers, plus a willingness to follow her empathy into a low-prestige problem (malaria in Vietnam, no PhD).
core_ideas.quote: Two statements are true. One, that most of that knowledge is rubbish. Two, that some of it is mind-blowingly great.

core_ideas.concept: Empathy Plus Curiosity Is The Strongest Research Package
core_ideas.explanation: Tu Youyou wasn't credentialed; she was simply moved by the suffering she witnessed in Vietnam, and that emotional pull pushed her to read the texts more carefully than anyone else. Ajay: 'The pure human flame burning in your breast.' This is a recurring EIE refrain — credentialism filters out exactly the people who carry both the empathy and the curiosity that produce breakthroughs.
core_ideas.quote: Hunger for knowledge arising out of empathy for the world. There's no better package in the world.

core_ideas.concept: Institutions Beat Stones — The Reconstruction Theorem
core_ideas.explanation: The Germany / Japan post-war story is presented as natural-experiment evidence. Both countries had every factory destroyed; both had the underlying brain power, books, and (crucially) restored institutional frameworks — Erhard's free-market reforms and a Weimar-style constitution in West Germany; American occupation and a pacifist constitution in Japan. Both rose like phoenixes. East Germany, with the same starting people but communist institutions, never recovered. Conclusion: physical capital can be rebuilt fast if human capital and institutions are right; the binding constraint is institutional, not material.
core_ideas.quote: There were enough people with the minds. And by the way, they hung on to records and they protected the shareholding of pre-war shareholders.

core_ideas.explanation: Stefan Zweig's chess prisoner playing himself reaches a high level — he beats a world champion once — but Amit reads the parable as having a ceiling. AlphaZero can self-play; humans cannot, not really. We need conversations: 'every game with somebody else is a conversation between two people where ideas are facing up against each other.' Mastery requires osmotic transmission of patterns from other minds. Solitary genius is a romantic myth.
core_ideas.quote: Just playing with himself he would never be able to go beyond a certain point.

core_ideas.explanation: Roughly half of the top-20 modern drugs derived from plants known to traditional peoples. Coffee was discovered by an Ethiopian shepherd watching his goats; gorillas teach aborigines which plants cure stomach upsets. Modern science refines, doses and industrialises this seed knowledge — but it doesn't generate it. As forest peoples vanish in a generation, an irreplaceable working laboratory of empirical biology is being silently destroyed. The episode treats this as a quiet emergency.
core_ideas.quote: It is really tragic how the knowledge of the forest in the hands of the aborigines is rapidly vanishing.

core_ideas.concept: If You Stop Doing It, You Stop Knowing It
core_ideas.explanation: The unifying lesson across silphium, Dhaka muslin, fogbank and the painted bench: knowledge that isn't actively practised decays. Documentation slows the decay; physical samples and archives slow it further; but only continuous use — by people, in workshops and labs and institutions — preserves the full body of know-how. This recasts education and apprenticeship not as transmission but as life-support for a fragile thing.
core_ideas.quote: If you stop actively doing something, the knowledge will be lost.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens by promising the gentle reader: 'we're going to scare the bujesis out of you.'

Amit on Tim Urban's experiment: 7.3 billion naked people on the planet. 'You could argue there are anyway, they're just putting some clothes on.' He follows it with Bob Dylan's line: 'even the president of the United States must stand naked while taking a bath.'

On Calcutta's retail scene feeling stuck in 1979: 'There was somebody with a physical weighing machine that looked like it was made in 1964, asking for one rupee coins to check your weight. I did that three times and my weight went down each time — because I was losing a one-rupee coin.'
Amit on Bengali achievements: a friend coined 'the big bong theory — that everything really started with big bongs as it were.'
The 1801 milliner satire: 'Madam, this is it. In these days, if you want to be well dressed, you have to be well undressed.'
Ajay's caveat about silphium dual-use: 'It was used as both an aphrodisiac and a contraceptive. So you're, like, completely covered out there.'

The painted-bench parable's punchline: the 93-year-old founder, asked why a guard stands eternal vigil over a random bench, looks up with wizened eyes — 'What are you saying? The paint hasn't dried yet.'

Pliny's prescription for a prolapse: 'When the gut protrudes and will not remain in its place, scrape the finest and most compact silphium into small pieces and apply as a cataplasm.' Amit, deadpan: 'You can see why this is of special interest.'
'I, Pencil' — Leonard Read's parable that no human knows how to make a pencil; the foundational text on dispersed knowledge.
Frederic Bastiat on 'How Do You Feed The City Of Paris?' — invoked alongside I, Pencil and Hayek as evidence that no one plans the city's food and yet it gets fed through prices.
Pliny the Elder's *Natural History*: 'Just one stalk has been found and it has been given to the Emperor Nero' — the historical sentence that fixes silphium's extinction in time.

Petronius in the *Satyricon* on early diaphanous fashion: 'a bride might as well stand naked' — invoked by Amit to show the long history of moral panic about see-through cloth, reaching back to Roman times.
'Probashi' — Ajay introduces the Bengali word for a Bengali who lives outside Bengal; he himself, despite his roots, is a probashi.
Ignaz Semmelweis — Amit alludes to an earlier episode about the obstetrician who discovered hand-washing in maternity wards, where ~10% of women died because no one knew about germ theory.
In 1933, Germany had more Nobel laureates than the United States — Ajay's recurring data point about how high Germany sat before the catastrophe.
